destination.title: Police Can Stop and Frisk You Without Arresting You

short06: Police can stop you and pat you down, even without arresting you.
All they need is reasonable suspicion, a little more than a hunch.
In 1968, a detective watched two men pace outside a store, again and again.
He patted them down, and found a gun.
The Supreme Court allowed it, eight to one.
A lower standard, stop and frisk, was born.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: The rule that allows it was written in 1968, and it began with one detective watching two men pace in front of a store window .
It is October 1963, in downtown Cleveland, Ohio.

If an officer can never check a person for a weapon until he already has proof of a crime, then the most dangerous moment of the job — the unknown person, the unseen gun — is also the moment the law leaves him most exposed.
The decision it wrote in 1968 tried to hold both truths at once, and that is exactly why it has been argued about ever since.
In 1968, by a vote of eight to one, the Supreme Court upheld the search .
The purpose is narrow: not to find evidence, but to make sure no one gets shot during the encounter.
That argument is not really a disagreement about the 1968 ruling.
